topics.answer: Hi, I'm Carlos! I'm a senior iOS developer based in Coimbra, Portugal. Ask me anything about my work, my apps or how I like to build things.
Thanks for stopping by, it was nice chatting! If you'd like to keep the conversation going, drop me a line at carlosanielrf@gmail.com.

Pretty much anything about my work: my job at Bosch, what I did before, Periplum and CoinPath (my own apps), my tech stack, how I approach architecture and testing, my career timeline, what kind of role I'm looking for, or how to get in touch. Just ask the way you would in person.

I'm a senior iOS developer, and I've been shipping apps to the App Store for {iosYears} years. I started on a B2B marketplace that launched in 20 countries, then a Portuguese C2C marketplace, and for the last {boschYears} years I've been at Bosch, working on the apps people use to control their home heating from their phone. In my own time I built two iOS apps, Periplum and CoinPath, each on my own from the first commit to the store listing.

Here's the short version:
2015–2018: Bachelor's in Multimedia, Instituto Superior Miguel Torga.
2018–2019: Web developer at Appsconcept (IPN, Coimbra), React and Angular.
2019–2021: iOS developer at Appsconcept, on a B2B marketplace in 20 countries and on CustoJusto.
2021–now: iOS developer at Bosch Thermotechnology in Aveiro, on four connected-heating apps.
On the side: Periplum and CoinPath, my own apps on the App Store.

questions: How many years of experience do you have?
How long have you been an iOS developer?
topics.answer: {iosYears} years as an iOS developer, since January 2019. Before that I spent a few months doing web development, starting in September 2018.

questions: What do you do at the moment?
topics.answer: I'm an iOS developer at Bosch Thermotechnology in Aveiro, and I've been there since July 2021. I build and maintain the connected-heating apps for four Bosch brands.

topics.chip: Which apps do you work on?
questions: Which apps do you work on at Bosch?
What Bosch apps have you built?
Tell me about Vulcano Connect and IVT Anywhere
topics.answer: There are four: HomeCom Easy, MyBuderus, Vulcano Connect and IVT Anywhere. At heart they all do the same thing, letting people control their home heating from their phone, and they all ship from one shared iOS codebase.

questions: How do you handle four brands in one codebase?
Tell me about the shared codebase
topics.answer: It's all one iOS codebase for the four brands. The hard part, and the interesting one, is making one interface work for a whole catalogue of appliance types and generations, and for people of all ages across lots of countries and languages.

questions: How does the app talk to the appliance?
topics.answer: Yes. I work on the part where the app talks to the actual heating appliance, and it has to get that right every time. When that link fails, people feel it at home, so I give it the same care as anything on screen.

questions: Do you have machine learning experience?
topics.answer: A bit, yes. At Bosch I tested a Core ML model that runs on the device and spots faults in an appliance by looking at its heating and cooling data.

questions: Where did you work before Bosch?
topics.answer: Before Bosch I was at Appsconcept, at IPN in Coimbra. I joined as a web developer in September 2018, moved to iOS in January 2019, and stayed until July 2021.

questions: Tell me about Agriaffaires and Truckscorner
What apps did you build from scratch?
topics.answer: That was my big from-scratch project at Appsconcept: a B2B marketplace that launched in 20 countries as three apps, MachineryZone, Agriaffaires and Truckscorner. Three business models on one shared codebase.

questions: Tell me about the app rating improvement
Have you improved an app's rating?
topics.answer: CustoJusto is a Portuguese C2C marketplace that I maintained. I went through the reviews, fixed the problems people kept mentioning, and the App Store rating went up two stars, to 4.5★.

questions: Have you worked with React or Angular?
topics.answer: Yes, that's actually where I started. From 2018 to 2019 I worked on a big-data dashboard in React and Angular that built charts tailored to each client, and it taught me how much analytics shapes a product. I also worked on an on-site AR preview tool for a construction company.
A little. I worked on a preview tool for a construction company: you pointed the camera at physical markers on site and saw foundations and structures that hadn't been built yet.

questions: Do you have a finance app?
Is CoinPath on the App Store?
Do you have a personal finance app?
topics.answer:
CoinPath is my personal finance app, and it just went live on the App Store. It brings spending, investments and net worth into one private place: you import bank statements (CSV or XLSX) with your own rules and duplicate detection, sync holdings from Interactive Brokers and Coinbase, split shared expenses, follow a budget rule like 50/30/20, and get a short monthly summary with one concrete thing to do.

It's local-first and works without an account. Like Periplum, I built it alone, from the first commit to the store listing.

questions: How does CoinPath keep data private?
topics.answer:
Privacy is the point of it. The ledger lives on the device in SwiftData. If you sign in with Apple or Google, an AES-256-GCM encrypted copy is kept in your account so a new phone can restore it, and signing out clears it from the device. Broker keys sit in the Keychain, and Face ID or a PIN can lock the app.

The monthly insights run on-device by default; AI is optional and uses your own API key. Under the hood it's SwiftUI, MVVM with protocol-backed services, and StoreKit 2 subscriptions behind a Remote Config flag. It needs iOS 18 and comes in English, Portuguese and Spanish.

questions: Tell me about your own app
Have you built an app alone?
Tell me about your travel app
topics.answer:
Periplum is my travel app. You capture the places you visit (a restaurant, a viewpoint, a trail) with notes, photos and location, organise them into trips, and share a trip with friends as a file or a PDF itinerary. It can also read an itinerary someone already wrote as a PDF and turn it into a trip, asking about anything it can't work out on its own.

I built it alone, from the design to the store listing. It's live in Portugal, Spain, France, Italy, the US and the UK, in five languages plus British English. My second app, CoinPath, a personal finance app, just launched too.

SwiftUI and SwiftData on iOS 18, compiled with Swift 6 strict concurrency set to complete. All the domain logic (filtering and sorting the catalogue, the sharing format, feed ranking, validation) lives in a local Swift package that only depends on Foundation, so it's quick to test and even builds on Linux.

Around it: widgets for quick capture on the Home Screen, Lock Screen and Control Center, App Intents for Shortcuts and Siri, Sign in with Apple and Google, a Firestore backup that only uploads what changed, a photo pipeline that never asks for full library access, and a PDF parser that reads an itinerary by its typography.

questions: Can I see your apps on the App Store?
Where can I download your apps?
topics.answer: Sure, here's everything I've shipped or maintained. The Bosch apps, Periplum and CoinPath are what I'm working on now; CustoJusto and the B2B marketplace apps are from 2019 to 2021.
Here's my stack, by area:

Swift and SwiftUI are what I use every day, and I have plenty of UIKit experience too. Along the way I've also worked with RxSwift, SwiftData, WidgetKit, App Intents, MapKit, PDFKit, StoreKit 2, Core ML and Swift Concurrency, on both iPhone and iPad.

Every day. Periplum compiles with Swift 6 strict concurrency set to complete, so a data race is a compile error rather than a bug someone finds in production. Sometimes that takes real work, like reducing a framework's response to a Sendable type before it crosses from a background task to the main actor. I use async/await in my day-to-day work too.

questions: Which programming languages do you know?
topics.answer: Mostly Swift. I also know Kotlin Multiplatform and JavaScript.

questions: Are you a mobile developer for both platforms?
topics.answer: iOS is my focus, and that's where my {iosYears} years are. Outside Swift I also know Kotlin Multiplatform and JavaScript.

questions: How do you structure an app?
topics.answer:
MVVM most of the time, and I've also used MVP, MVC and VIPER where they fit. What matters more to me is where the business logic lives. In Periplum it's a local Swift package with no UI frameworks, so it's fast to test and can't get tangled with views. CoinPath is MVVM with @Observable view models talking to protocol-backed services (the ledger, statement import, broker sync), which keeps each piece easy to swap in tests.

For dependencies I've worked with SPM, CocoaPods and Carthage.

questions: How do you test your apps?
topics.answer:
Periplum has 449 automated tests written with Swift Testing. The domain package can be tested on its own, without a simulator, and a pre-push hook runs the whole suite plus a check that every string exists in all five languages, so a broken build or a missing translation never leaves my machine. GitHub Actions runs the same script on every release tag, and Xcode Cloud builds what goes to TestFlight.

At Bosch I test the REST endpoints against the product requirements every release, so if an API contract drifts, we catch it before customers do.

I work with REST APIs designed in Swagger, and I check API contracts before a release, not after, so any drift gets caught before customers see it. On my own apps I've also integrated third-party APIs directly, like Interactive Brokers' Flex reports and Coinbase in CoinPath.

questions: Which CI tools do you use?
topics.answer:
On my own apps, a pre-push hook runs the tests locally, GitHub Actions runs the tests and text checks on release tags, and Xcode Cloud builds every TestFlight and App Store build from a version tag. In previous jobs I've also used Jenkins and Travis CI.

I take apps all the way through release myself: privacy manifest, App Store Connect, screenshots generated from demo data, and store listings in several languages.

Yes. I've worked with designers through Zeplin and documented things in Confluence, and I use Firebase Analytics and Crashlytics to see what's really happening in the app. Working on analytics dashboards early on showed me how much data shapes product decisions.

Quite a lot. Periplum speaks five languages plus British English through String Catalogs, and a script fails the push if any string is missing in any language, if a plural is built by gluing an "s", or if the French switches between tu and vous. CoinPath ships in English, Portuguese and Spanish.

The Bosch apps serve users across many countries and languages from one codebase, and the B2B marketplace launched in 20 countries.
